title: Topology-Aware Workload Scheduling with NVIDIA Topograph | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: NVIDIA released Topograph, an open-source toolkit that discovers cluster network topology across clouds and on-prem fabrics and feeds it to Kubernetes, Slurm, and Slinky schedulers so AI workloads are placed for locality; it's part of NVIDIA's push to own the full 'AI factory' orchestration stack, not just silicon, reinforced by its December 2025 acquisition of Slurm-maker SchedMD.

insights.claim: NVIDIA frames AI factories as power-limited systems, meaning GPU workload placement efficiency (not just raw GPU count) determines delivered value, since poor placement leaves power-provisioned GPUs idle while waiting on data.
insights.speaker: Dmitry Shmulevich
insights.so_what: Investors should read GPU cluster efficiency (tokens/watt, utilization) as a real cost/throughput lever for AI infra spend, not a minor operational detail -- it directly affects the economics hyperscalers get per GPU dollar.
insights.quote: AI factories are power-limited systems that deliver maximum value when fully optimized.

insights.claim: Poor GPU workload placement fragments topology domains and forces traffic across shared links, which reduces throughput, raises job costs, and leaves GPUs consuming provisioned power without advancing the workload.
insights.speaker: Dmitry Shmulevich
insights.so_what: This is a direct cost-per-token driver at scale; software that mitigates it (like Topograph) has real economic value for anyone running large GPU clusters, supporting demand for NVIDIA's orchestration-layer tools alongside its hardware.
insights.quote: Poor workload placement fragments topology domains and forces traffic across shared links, reducing throughput, raising job costs, and leaving GPUs consuming provisioned power while waiting on data without advancing the workload.

insights.claim: NVIDIA NVLink provides 1.8 TB/s of bidirectional bandwidth per GPU in its fifth generation (Blackwell, e.g. GB200/GB300) and 3.6 TB/s per GPU in its sixth generation (Vera Rubin), delivered through a dedicated non-blocking, all-to-all NVLink Switch fabric.
insights.speaker: Dmitry Shmulevich
insights.so_what: The doubling of per-GPU NVLink bandwidth from Blackwell to Vera Rubin is a concrete generational roadmap data point supporting NVIDIA's continued interconnect performance lead versus merchant-silicon/Ethernet-only scale-up alternatives.
insights.quote: NVIDIA NVLink provides 1.8 TB/s of bidirectional bandwidth per GPU in its fifth generation (NVIDIA Blackwell, such as GB200/GB300) and 3.6 TB/s per GPU in its sixth generation (Vera Rubin)

insights.claim: Modern NVIDIA Quantum InfiniBand ports can achieve up to 800 Gb/s, positioned as the scale-out fabric complementing NVLink's rack-scale scale-up bandwidth.
insights.speaker: Dmitry Shmulevich
insights.so_what: Confirms NVIDIA's two-tier networking stack (NVLink for scale-up, InfiniBand/Spectrum-X for scale-out) as a specific, defensible performance moat that customers must design around.
insights.quote: Modern NVIDIA Quantum InfiniBand ports can achieve up to 800 Gb/s

insights.claim: Topograph is built on two decoupled concepts: a 'provider' that discovers topology from cloud APIs or on-prem systems and normalizes it into a canonical model, and an 'engine' that translates that model into scheduler-specific output (Kubernetes labels, Slurm config, Slinky ConfigMaps, NFD resources, or topology JSON).
insights.speaker: Dmitry Shmulevich
insights.so_what: The provider/engine abstraction is a reusable design pattern that lets NVIDIA add new clouds or schedulers cheaply, accelerating ecosystem coverage and stickiness across heterogeneous infrastructure.

insights.claim: Topograph continuously regenerates its topology view via five components (API server, node observer, node data broker, provider, engine) so schedulers work from current cluster state rather than a manually maintained snapshot, with a default 15-second request-aggregation delay to reduce redundant work during event bursts.
insights.speaker: Dmitry Shmulevich
insights.so_what: Automating topology freshness removes a manual-maintenance burden that otherwise degrades placement quality as clusters scale and churn, which is a real operational cost saved for large GPU cluster operators.
insights.quote: The aggregation delay is required; 15 seconds is typical. Repeated identical requests reset a trailing timer and are processed once, reducing redundant work during bursts of cluster events.

insights.claim: The default Kubernetes scheduler does not discover physical interconnect hierarchy on its own; Topograph closes that gap by publishing topology as node labels that native pod affinity and topology-aware schedulers can consume.
insights.speaker: Dmitry Shmulevich
insights.so_what: Highlights a real gap in open-source Kubernetes that NVIDIA is filling with proprietary-adjacent tooling, a classic pattern for building dependency on NVIDIA's software layer even where hardware plays are equal (e.g., non-NVIDIA GPUs on K8s still lack this).
insights.quote: The default Kubernetes scheduler doesn’t discover physical interconnect hierarchy.

insights.claim: Topograph has working integrations with cloud providers Google Cloud, Lambda, Nebius, Nscale, Crusoe, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, with more cloud and colocation providers in development, plus on-prem support for InfiniBand, Spectrum-X, and Multi-Node NVLink domains.
insights.speaker: Dmitry Shmulevich
insights.so_what: NVIDIA's orchestration software already spans essentially every major GPU cloud/neocloud, meaning it can capture scheduling-layer value and influence regardless of which cloud wins GPU capacity share -- a horizontal moat independent of hardware sales.
insights.locator: A common model across environments / Environment and Engine Support table

insights.claim: NVIDIA acquired SchedMD, the developer of the Slurm workload manager and Slinky (Slurm-on-Kubernetes), in December 2025.
insights.speaker: Dmitry Shmulevich
insights.so_what: This acquisition is a concrete, material data point: NVIDIA now owns the dominant HPC/AI job scheduler outright, extending its stack from chips and networking into cluster orchestration software -- a vertical-integration move investors should weight when assessing NVIDIA's software-driven moat and pricing power.
insights.quote: Slinky, developed by SchedMD, runs Slurm on Kubernetes. NVIDIA acquired SchedMD in December 2025.

insights.claim: KAI Scheduler, used for topology-aware gang scheduling with Topograph, is a CNCF Sandbox project that was donated to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation by NVIDIA.
insights.speaker: Dmitry Shmulevich
insights.so_what: NVIDIA is using open-source donation/governance (CNCF) as a distribution strategy for scheduling infrastructure, similar to how CUDA-adjacent tooling built developer lock-in -- watch for KAI Scheduler becoming a de facto standard that favors NVIDIA-aware topology signals.
insights.quote: KAI Scheduler (a CNCF Sandbox project donated by NVIDIA)
insights.locator: Using KAI Scheduler for Topology-Aware Gang Scheduling

insights.claim: Kubernetes 1.36 introduced only alpha-stage native topology-aware workload scheduling (via KEP-5732), with upstream beta work still ongoing and no committed release timeline.
insights.speaker: Dmitry Shmulevich
insights.so_what: Native Kubernetes topology-awareness is years behind what NVIDIA already ships in Topograph/KAI Scheduler, giving NVIDIA a multi-year head start to entrench its scheduling stack before open-source K8s catches up.
insights.quote: Kubernetes 1.36 also introduced alpha topology-aware workload scheduling through KEP-5732. Upstream beta work is ongoing; consult the enhancement tracker rather than depending on a specific future release.

insights.claim: Topograph is open source (hosted at dsx-ai-factory/topograph on GitHub) with an open provider interface so operators can add support for their own environment and contribute it upstream.
insights.speaker: Dmitry Shmulevich
insights.so_what: Open-sourcing the discovery layer while NVIDIA controls the reference implementation and downstream integrations (KAI, DRA, DSX OS) is a low-cost way to seed adoption broadly while retaining influence over the de facto standard -- a pattern to watch across NVIDIA's software portfolio.
insights.locator: A common model across environments / Getting started

themes.theme: DSX OS: building a full AI-factory software stack

insights.claim: Topograph operates within NVIDIA's DSX OS cluster orchestration layer alongside Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) and KAI Scheduler, and the post explicitly ties topology-aware scheduling to improving 'AI factory efficiency, tokens per watt, and cost.'
insights.speaker: Dmitry Shmulevich
insights.so_what: Signals NVIDIA is assembling a proprietary/open-source hybrid 'operating system' for AI data centers spanning scheduling, resource allocation, and networking -- an expanding software surface area (beyond GPUs) that could become a durable, higher-margin revenue and lock-in layer as AI factories scale.
insights.quote: Through KAI Scheduler, Kueue, and native Kubernetes, the map improves AI factory efficiency, tokens per watt, and cost.
